claims.text: High configurational entropy in HEAs promotes kinetically favorable surface segregation of oxide-forming elements.
Aluminum can act as an oxide-forming element in Al-containing HEAs.
Surface segregation of oxide-forming elements rapidly nucleates a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
Formation and retention of the proposed protective oxide scale enhance oxidation resistance.
The high configurational entropy decreases the energetic barrier for diffusion of oxide-forming elements toward the surface.
The high configurational entropy decreases the energetic barrier for surface segregation of oxide-forming elements.
Surface-enriched oxide-forming elements react with oxygen to produce an oxide scale.
The resulting oxide scale is dense and adherent.
The oxide scale limits further oxygen diffusion into the alloy.
Increasing the concentration of the selected oxide-forming element causes faster formation of a protective oxide scale.
Increasing the concentration of the selected oxide-forming element reduces oxidation rates relative to a lower-concentration baseline.
Reduced oxidation rates would be observed as lower temporal weight gain.
The mechanism requires temperatures high enough to activate diffusion.
The mechanism ceases to govern when severe scale spallation or bulk-alloy degradation dominates.
The proposed oxidation mechanism is not applicable under non-oxidizing conditions.
Samples differing in oxide-former concentration should be exposed to the same high-temperature oxidizing environment and compared by weight gain, surface analysis, and oxide-scale microscopy.
A lack of a statistically significant difference in oxide-scale formation or protective quality between enhanced and baseline samples would falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of preferential surface segregation of the oxide-forming element in the enhanced sample would falsify the hypothesis.
